newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE-Israelis gird for fear of war with Syria.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Israelis gird for fear of war with Syria.

text.p: Take a seat on a Golan Heights hilltop known as Har Bental and you might be in a perfect position to view Israel's next war with Syria.
The hill on the eastern ridge of the Golan overlooks a string of valleys linking Syria to the heights it lost to Israel in a war nearly 30 years ago and wants back.

Israel, fearing its neighbour is on a warpath, has kept thousands of troops on high alert in the Golan Heights since Syria moved a large part of its garrison in Lebanon towards the Israeli border in September.

With little prospect of wrenching the heights through diplomacy from newly elected Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Syria's 27-year president Hafez al-Assad has refused to resume peace talks, prompting speculation he will try to reclaim the Golan by force.
"If Syria were to launch an all-out war against Israel, it would begin here," said reserve lieutenant-colonel Amitai Shelem, pointing to the valleys below.
"This is the only area where Syria can move tanks into the Golan Heights," he said.

Hundreds of Syrian tanks crossed the border here in 1973 in the last major confrontation, charging deep into the heights -- its widest point is less than 20 km (12 miles) long -- before being pushed back by Israeli forces.

Anti-tank ditches now crisscross the high-altitude Golan to impede a Syrian offensive. Surveillance installations on the Hermon, the highest peak in the area, let Israel look and listen deep into Syrian territory.
The Golan is dotted with water reservoirs built since the last war in part for military purposes -- they would allow Israel to flood battlegrounds during war and immobilise opposing forces.
Israeli-Syrian tensions have soared since September over signs of a pending Syrian military strike against the Jewish state.

Among the indications were Syria's redeployment of 12,000 troops in Lebanon to within striking range of the Golan and a series of Syrian military exercises which, unlike in previous years, included offensive drills.
Israel holds annual war games of its own on the Golan Heights which it captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

Israeli security sources said the most disturbing sign across the border was the participation in manoeuvres of Syrian paratroop and commando units that form part of Assad's own protection force and rarely leave Damascus.

Israeli intelligence officials told parliament's Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee last month that war with Damascus was a possibility and analysts speculated a Syrian assault would fall between the U.S. election and the start of winter when rain and mud made a ground war difficult.
But not everyone agrees with the assessment.

"It looks to me like an artificial tension resulting either from a misunderstanding or an immaturity among some leaders here in the Middle East," said retired Major-General Uri Saguy, head of military intelligence until last year.
"I don't believe, I don't estimate that the Syrians are preparing for something different from their usual policy," he told Reuters.
Saguy in 1991 was among the first Israeli officials to identify a change in Syria's policy towards the Jewish state -- a strategic decision to get back the Golan through peace talks rather than war.

But negotiations launched later that year at a landmark Madrid conference have stumbled over the fate of the Golan. Now the Syrian leader, 66, may want to challenge the young and untested Netanyahu, 47.

"President Assad is a master in combining force and diplomacy," Middle East expert Itamar Rabinovich, who headed Israel's negotiating team with Syria under the previous left-centre government, told Reuters.

Israel has long accused Syria of encouraging Islamic militant attacks on the Jewish state from Lebanon to gain leverage in peace talks, but the border with Syria on the Golan Heights has been Israel's quietest.

Some analysts say Assad may simply step up the campaign against Israel in Lebanon where Syria maintains 35,000 troops and a tight grip over the government and where Israeli soldiers patrol a 15-km (nine-mile) wide occupation zone.
Others think he may make a grab for the Golan in a message to Israel that 23 years of tranquillity do not mean Syria has given up on recovering the heights.
"That's precisely the kind of equation we want to avoid...I hope the government has a well-thought-out strategy for dealing with this," Rabinovich said.
